verdict: Caution — lend selectively to cold-chain and processing units with verified receivables; avoid pure orchard-level and floriculture exposure until price and incentive data are in hand.
title: Srinagar horticulture & floriculture: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**This is a harvest-to-cash business, not a manufacturing one: apples and flowers are picked in a short window, then either sold at once or held in cold storage against a later price.** Cash leaves the borrower at harvest (labour, packing, freight) and comes back only when the crop is sold — so the working-capital cycle is the whole credit story. Cost is dominated by picking, carting and storage rent; pricing power sits with the buyer, not the grower. **So when a proposal lands, check the borrower's own harvest-to-sale calendar and the share of crop that goes into storage versus spot sale; if the storage share is high, ask what price they are betting on and who has agreed to buy.**

## What has changed now
**Cold stores in Kashmir are filling up because growers are holding stock hoping for better prices [1] — that is a price bet funded by storage rent, and it lengthens the cash cycle.** Separately, 43 industrial incentive cases worth about ₹1,800 crore are pending with the government, and the association has taken this to the LG [2]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's cash flow depends on a pending incentive claim; if it does, ask for the claim status and treat that receivable as collect-from-customer until disbursed.** On the positive side, Northern Railway is offering a 50% concession on round-trip fares for fruit consignments [3] — that lowers outbound freight cost for traders who rail their crop.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue cold-chain operators, packhouses and fruit traders who move volume by rail, and processing units with a real offtake contract.** The rail concession [3] and the cold-store build-out [1] both point to organised storage and logistics as the segment where cash is most visible. **Avoid pure orchard-level lending and floriculture until you have price data — the listed floriculture peer shows sales up 40.95% to ₹13.18 crore in March 2026 but a net loss of ₹2.15 crore and negative EBITDA of ₹0.24 crore [6], so revenue growth alone is not repayment capacity.** Note the peer is a national listed company, not a Srinagar unit; local floriculture data is thin and must be collected from customer.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the crop, not the balance sheet: sanction limits tied to storage receipts and rail consignments, with a monthly stock-and-receipt statement as the drawing condition.** Take every month: cold-store rent receipts, rail booking confirmations, and a stock statement reconciled to the godown. **If the borrower cannot produce storage receipts, ask for the godown's own issue register.** Keep tenors inside one storage season and avoid bullet repayment against a hoped-for price.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for stock sitting past the normal sale window, rent arrears at the cold store, and any proposal that leans on the pending ₹1,800 crore incentive pool [2] for repayment.** If rail bookings stop while storage rent keeps accruing, ask why the crop is not moving. **If the borrower's sale price falls below the storage-plus-freight cost, treat it as a stress signal and re-size the limit.**
watch: Stock held past normal sale window -> ask for sale plan and re-size limit
Bookings stop while rent accrues -> ask why crop is not moving; treat as stress
Claim still pending -> exclude from cash flow; collect from customer
Realised sale price vs storage plus freight cost (monthly)
Price below cost -> re-size limit and review tenor
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
